metadata.title: Reading as a catalyst for creative attitude: evidence from rural China and the cognitive pathways linking literacy and innovation

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses a three-stage sampling design to select rural public primary schools and intact fourth-grade classes in Jiangxi Province (120 schools; 3424 students across three waves). The paper does not report the use of PIRLS-style sampling weights or any explicit complex-survey weighting variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) in the estimation. Because the analysis is based on panel regressions with school and year fixed effects (and an instrumental-variables approach), the manuscript does not document whether survey weights were applied to produce population-representative estimates. Analysts using the underlying dataset should treat the results as conditional on the sampled rural schools/classes unless weights are provided in the data release; no replicate-weight variance estimation (BRR/jackknife) is described.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is an attitudinal creative attitude score from the Creativity Attitude Survey (CAS), and the reading measures are derived from a PIRLS-referenced reading test and related sub-dimensions; the paper does not describe any plausible-value (PV) generation or PV-based scaling. Missing-data handling is also not documented beyond stating that the final dataset includes complete observations after attrition and missing data, without specifying the rule (e.g., listwise deletion vs. imputation). This is a reporting gap because the study’s longitudinal panel and IV/robustness analyses are sensitive to how missingness is treated.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample consists of fourth-grade students from rural public primary schools in Jiangxi Province, China, selected via three-stage sampling: (1) three underdeveloped poverty-stricken counties, (2) stratified random selection of rural public primary schools within counties (120 schools total), and (3) selection of up to two fourth-grade classes per school (randomly choosing two when more than two exist), including all students present in the selected classes on survey day. The longitudinal panel includes three waves (May 2015, May 2016, May 2017) using the same instruments and fixed administration order; the final dataset includes complete observations for 3424 students after accounting for attrition and missing data.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS-referenced Grade 4 Reading test (2011 framework), rural Jiangxi China (2015-2017 waves)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-way fixed effects (3-year panel): coefficient = 0.298 standard deviations; OLS by year: 2015 = 0.190 SD, 2016 = 0.328 SD, 2017 = 1.393 SD. IV (2SLS): coefficient = 0.403; weak instrument test F = 25.98. Robustness (lagged reading): coefficient = 0.360; R-squared (two-way FE) = 0.157.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS-referenced Grade 4 reading test data from rural Jiangxi China across 2015–2017 waves, the study leveraged standardized reading scores alongside household books, school library availability, class book corner, and parental education to predict students’ creative attitude (CAS), finding a positive association (two-way fixed effects coefficient = 0.298 SD) and a larger IV estimate (0.403) suggesting stronger effects after addressing endogeneity. This indicates that improving reading achievement in under-resourced rural primary schools may be a practical lever for strengthening children’s creative attitudes, though the study’s causal claims remain limited by endogeneity assumptions and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS-referenced Grade 4 Reading test (2011 framework), rural Jiangxi China (2015-2017 waves)
main_findings.target_variable: Creative attitude score (CAS) — reading ability dimensions
main_findings.performance_metrics: Robustness/ability-dimension models (Table 4): lagged reading coefficient = 0.360***; retrieval ability = 0.271***; inferential ability = 0.251***; integration ability = 0.225***; evaluation ability = 0.215***. Observations range: 6848 to 10,272 depending on model.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS-referenced Grade 4 reading test data from rural Jiangxi China, the study leveraged retrieval, inferential, integration, and evaluation reading abilities (plus reading speed as part of the comprehension/logical pathway) to predict creative attitude (CAS), finding that all four reading dimensions are positively associated with creative attitude in robustness checks. This indicates that curriculum and instruction should target multiple components of reading comprehension—not only overall reading performance—to support creative-attitude development in rural settings.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS-referenced Grade 4 Reading test (2011 framework), rural Jiangxi China (2015-2017 waves)
main_findings.target_variable: Creative attitude score (CAS) — heterogeneity in reading effects
main_findings.performance_metrics: Heterogeneity (Table 6, two-way FE with controls): reading lessons vs none: 0.366*** vs 0.279***; family rich vs poor: 0.315*** vs 0.271***; reading room vs none: 0.314*** vs 0.271***; reading activities vs none: 0.378*** vs 0.284***; bottom 20% assets vs top 20%: 0.266*** vs 0.317***; bottom 25% reading scores vs top 25%: 0.375*** vs 0.163***. Coefficient difference p-values reported (e.g., <0.01***, 0.032**, 0.034**).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS-referenced Grade 4 reading test data from rural Jiangxi China, the study leveraged contextual supports (reading lessons, family reading atmosphere, reading room availability, reading-activity participation) and resource/position indicators (household assets level and reading-score ranking) to predict creative attitude, finding that the reading–creative attitude link is stronger in more supportive environments and among lower-performing students. This indicates that reading-focused interventions should be paired with family and school reading-support structures to maximize creative-attitude gains and reduce disparities.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS-referenced Grade 4 Reading test (2011 framework), rural Jiangxi China (2015-2017 waves)
main_findings.target_variable: Creative attitude mechanisms (self-efficacy, reading behavior, comprehension/logical abilities)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Mechanism analysis (Table 5): reading scores → reading confidence = 0.202***; → imagination = 0.033***; → sharing reading experiences = 0.116***; → reading with friends = 0.048***; → books shared by friends = 0.085***; → video game time = -0.077***; → reading speed = 0.153***; → standardized maths scores = 0.304***. Observations ~10,032–10,272; R-squared varies (0.045 to 0.411).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS-referenced Grade 4 reading test data from rural Jiangxi China, the study leveraged standardized reading scores to predict creative-attitude-related mediators—reading confidence/imagination, collaborative reading behaviors, and comprehension/logical indicators (reading speed and maths performance)—finding positive effects on self-efficacy and reading behaviors and a negative association with video game time. This indicates that strengthening reading achievement may foster creative attitudes by building confidence, encouraging engaged peer reading, and improving comprehension and logical reasoning, suggesting multi-component intervention designs rather than reading-only exposure.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses a three-year longitudinal panel (2015–2017) of 3424 fourth-grade students from 120 rural primary schools in Jiangxi Province, China, to examine how reading achievement relates to creative attitude measured by the Creativity Attitude Survey (CAS). Reading achievement is assessed with a PIRLS-referenced Grade 4 reading test aligned to China’s curriculum, including overall standardized reading scores and four comprehension dimensions (retrieval, inferential, integration, evaluation). The main results come from two-way fixed effects models (school and year fixed effects), showing a positive association between reading and creative attitude (0.298 SD), supported by an instrumental-variables estimate using peers’ average standardized reading scores (0.403; first-stage F=25.98). Robustness checks using lagged reading and reading-dimension models also yield positive coefficients, and mechanism/heterogeneity analyses indicate stronger effects in supportive reading environments. Limitations include reliance on IV assumptions for endogeneity, no documented survey-weight use, and missing-data handling not fully specified.
